title: Modern close: saints now
hook: holiness keeps showing up in every generation, including this one

segments.voice: Yesterday, new movements: a hearth in a bomb shelter, students in Rome, a war ended by talks. Your line was laypeople lead. When does the group you looked up meet next? Day nine hundred forty-six.

This stretch of the path began in a French village, with a country priest, the Curé of Ars, hearing confessions from morning until night. Since then: a priest among the lepers of Molokai. Bakhita, sold as a slave and later a Canossian sister. A young Carmelite writing Story of a Soul. A friar in a starvation cell at Auschwitz. A mother named Gianna. An archbishop at the altar in San Salvador. A pope in an empty square. A teenager with a website. Today closes the modern Church with one question, asked plainly: are there saints now?
screen: `FROM A VILLAGE PRIEST IN ARS…` → `…TO A TEENAGER WITH A WEBSITE.` → `ARE THERE SAINTS NOW?`

segments.voice: First, the Church's own answer. The Second Vatican Council gave a whole chapter of its teaching on the Church to what it called the universal call to holiness: every baptized person, not only priests and religious, is called to be holy, in a kitchen, an office, a hospital ward. Saint Paul says it to the Thessalonians, in the Douay-Rheims: "For this is the will of God, your sanctification." Sanctification means being made holy. Not someday, and not only for experts. Second, the saints next door. Pope Francis wrote a letter on holiness in which he spoke of the saints next door: parents raising their children with love, people working hard to support their families, the sick, elderly religious who keep smiling. Holiness, he wrote in effect, is found among our neighbors. Third, canonized and not. When the Church canonizes someone, it declares that this person is with God and can be held up as a model. But the Church does not teach that heaven holds only the canonized. The feast of All Saints honors the whole crowd, named and unnamed. And some people in this stretch of the path, like Dorothy Day, still have causes open; the Church hasn't finished looking. Fourth, they're still here. In Catholic belief the saints are not gone but alive in God, joined with the living in what the creed calls the communion of saints. Catholics ask for their prayers the way they'd ask a friend. So the line for today means two things at once. The saints of the past are alive in God. And, the Church teaches, new ones are walking around now, in this generation, mostly unnoticed, maybe on your street.
screen: `A CALL TO HOLINESS FOR EVERYONE.` · `THE SAINTS NEXT DOOR.` · `CANONIZED, AND NOT.` · `THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS.` · then, large: `THIS IS THE WILL OF GOD, YOUR SANCTIFICATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a holy person you know. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind whose goodness you've seen up close: a grandparent, a nurse, a neighbor, a teacher, a friend who keeps showing up. Not a perfect person. Just someone good in a way that stays with you. Picture one ordinary moment of theirs: their hands at work, a phrase they always say, the way they make room for people. Stay with that moment. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, simply be grateful for them, slowly. The bell holds the time.

Communio sanctorum, Latin for the communion of saints. The end of this stretch on the modern Church, from the Curé of Ars to a teenager with a website: holiness showing up in every generation, including this one.
Your line: they're still here. Today, tell the person you thought of one good thing you've seen in them, plainly, without making a speech. Day nine hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate All Saints' Day for the holy dead known and unknown, ask the saints for their prayers, and in parishes and families tell the stories of holy people they have known.
